Explain like I'm a retard:

What is systemd?

Linux is all about small packages that do a very specific thing. They inherently specialize in that one thing, and tend to do a good job of it. Your cp function ONLY copies files/folders, and nothing else... your rm function ONLY removes files/folders, and nothing else... your mcdir ONLY creates directories, nothing else... and you get the point.

Back in the day, there was a package that monitored your background processes, which are called daemons in Linux. This daemon manager was called SysVInit since it initialized the system daemons. Well, as time went on, SysVInit became more-and-more patched as new "features" came out. USB hot-plugging became a thing, serial consoles and serial/SCSI cards became less of a thing, and computing changed, overall. All of these massive changes led to SysVInit becoming a hot mess, so the quest to make a new, better daemon manager was set.

Many were created: some were good, some were bad, and many just got washed out over time. One daemon manager that stood above the rest was Systemd, which was fast, lightweight, and capable. So, it became widely adopted.

Then the problems began: Pottering (the creator of Systemd) started absorbing other packages into Systemd... Contradicting the Linux mantra of small, specialized packages. Soon, Systemd ran your boot manager, networking, su, and other critical system packages. It has become so convoluted and bloated that it has almost became it's own system.

And package maintainers love that fact, as they can treat it as it's own system. Instead of packaging your program for Debian, Ubuntu, Slackware, Arch, Gentoo, and a litany of other distros, you just package it with Systemd and let Systemd take care of all of your dependencies! This made Systemd spread like wildfire!

"So, what's the problem," you might be asking...

Well, since it's gobbled up so many other packages, and violated the Linux mantra, when one thing breaks... IT ALL BREAKS!

Also, when your system crashes, you'd probably like to go to your logs to see what happened, right? Well, Systemd stores it's logs in binary, so those are probably garbage now... corrupted with the failed system.

Every single problem I've had, in the last two years, has been related to Systemd. For instance: Linux had its own power manager. If you download a new one, it took a backseat and relinquishes power to your new preferred/downloaded power manager... and things ran smoothly. But now, Systemd wants to run your power, as it's absorbed Linux's power manager... So, instead of relinquishing power to the new PM, Systemd "fights" with it, and your laptop never goes to sleep, hibernates, or works correctly... That's just how Systemd is.

Ultimately, Systemd looks like it's trying to become its own version of Linux, and regulate itself. It's well on its way to taking over all of the important tasks Linux runs, and will probably grow exponentially when Linus dies.
